stem: During a rapid IV vancomycin infusion, a client develops pruritus and erythema of the face, neck, and upper torso. What should the nurse do first?

options.A: Stop the vancomycin infusion and assess the client
options.B: Continue the infusion at the same rate because the reaction is expected
options.C: Increase the infusion rate so the dose finishes sooner
options.D: Permanently label the client as having an IgE-mediated vancomycin allergy without further evaluation

rationale: Current vancomycin prescribing information identifies pruritus and erythema of the face, neck, and upper body during rapid administration as a vancomycin infusion reaction. The label directs clinicians to stop the infusion if a reaction occurs because stopping it usually results in prompt cessation. Vancomycin should generally be infused over 60 minutes or longer to reduce infusion-reaction risk.
educational_objective: Recognize a vancomycin infusion reaction and stop the infusion promptly when characteristic flushing or pruritus develops during administration.
source_locator: Warnings and Precautions, Section 5.1 Infusion Reactions; Dosage and Administration, Section 2.1
source_claim_supported: Rapid IV vancomycin can cause a vancomycin infusion reaction with pruritus and erythema of the face, neck, and upper body; if a reaction occurs, stop the infusion, and administer vancomycin over at least 60 minutes to reduce risk.
correction_summary: Replaced outdated terminology and corrected the intervention from merely slowing an ongoing symptomatic infusion to the current label-directed first action of stopping the infusion. Removed cue-heavy explanatory distractors.
audit_findings: A directly matches the current FDA-label instruction. B and C would continue or worsen exposure during an active reaction. D overcalls an infusion-rate reaction as confirmed IgE-mediated allergy. No second defensible answer remains.
